# The Hateful Immortals

## A Documentary Account of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage, 1847–2024

### Compiled and Annotated by Dr. Amelia Thornton, Department of Anomalous Historical Studies, Reed College

---

## I. The Vow

The oldest artifact in the Greenbriar-Chen Archive is a single sheet of cotton rag paper, eight inches by ten, folded twice along its length and stored for most of its existence inside a copy of *Dombey and Son* that Margaret Greenbriar purchased secondhand from a shop on Milk Street, Boston, in either late 1847 or early 1848.[^1] The paper bears the couple's wedding vows, written in Margaret's hand. Her penmanship, in the original inscription, is careful, round, and slightly trembling—whether from emotion or from the cold of the church vestry, where she appears to have transcribed the vows from memory immediately following the ceremony, we cannot determine. What we can determine, because Margaret Greenbriar-Chen's memory was then and would remain for the next 177 years as involuntary and as total as a daguerreotype plate, is that the transcription is exact. She would later confirm—in a letter to her cousin Hester, in 1904—that she could still hear Reverend Alcott's adenoidal drone, still feel where the whalebone of her corset dug into her left hip, still smell the particular admixture of tallow candle and James's borrowed pomade that constituted, for her, the olfactory signature of her wedding day.

[^1]: Margaret's marginalia on the flyleaf of the novel reads: "Purchased Nov. or Dec. A poor book by a great author. James likes it, which is diagnostic." Whether diagnostic of James's taste or of the novel's quality, she does not specify. This is characteristic.

The marriage itself was, by the standards of its time and place, a minor scandal and a major curiosity. Margaret Greenbriar was the third daughter of Ezra Greenbriar, a middlingly successful dealer in dry goods whose family had been in Massachusetts since before the Revolution—a fact he mentioned, per Margaret's later account, "at minimum twice per meal and thrice on Sundays." James Chen was the son of Chen Wei-Lin, a merchant who had arrived in Boston via San Francisco in 1839 and established a modest but reputable import business on the waterfront. The union was not illegal, as Massachusetts had no anti-miscegenation statute, but it was sufficiently unusual that the *Boston Evening Transcript* noted it in a three-line item under the heading "Nuptials of an Uncommon Character."[^2]

[^2]: The item's full text: "Married, on the 14th inst., at the First Congregational Church, Miss Margaret Greenbriar, of this city, to Mr. James Chen, also of this city, in a ceremony attended by a small number of family and friends. The groom is of the Chinese nation. The bride wore blue." The final sentence has the quality of a reporter who has exhausted his interest in the subject.

Neither bride nor groom, at the time of the wedding, fully understood what they were.

James's ability had manifested eleven months earlier, during a catastrophic boiler explosion at the Lowell textile mill where he had been conducting an inventory of imported silks for his father's firm. The blast killed nine workers and sent a fragment of cast iron through James's chest with sufficient force to embed itself in a load-bearing pillar six feet behind him. He was pronounced dead at the scene by a millhand who had seen quite enough death to know what it looked like. Twenty minutes later, James walked out of the wreckage under his own power, his shirt ruined, his chest bearing a wound that, by the time a physician examined him that evening, had already closed to a livid pink seam. James told his father it was "a near thing." He told Margaret, whom he was then courting, that he had been "extraordinarily lucky." Whether he believed this, or had already begun to suspect the truth, his surviving documents do not reveal. James Chen's relationship with the written word was, from the beginning, one of mutual wariness.[^3]

[^3]: His earliest surviving diary entry, dated March 1847, reads in its entirety: "Fine weather. Visited the Greenbriars. Margaret is clever. Her father less so." This is, by the standards of James's later diaries, practically a monograph.

Margaret's ability announced itself more gradually and, to her family, more disturbingly. She had always possessed what her mother, in a letter to a sister in Hartford, called "an unsettling habit of recollection"—an ability to reproduce conversations verbatim days after the fact, to recall what every person in a room had been wearing, to correct her father's customers on the quantities and prices of transactions they had themselves forgotten. In childhood this had been regarded as a parlor trick, then as an impertinence. By adolescence her mother had begun asking her to please stop. In the months following her engagement to James, the ability intensified—whether through some physiological trigger or simply through Margaret's growing willingness to acknowledge it—until it became clear that she was not merely remembering with unusual accuracy but remembering *everything*, involuntarily, permanently, in sensory detail that encompassed tone of voice, ambient sound, the pressure of fabric against skin, the precise slant of light through a window at a given hour on a given day. She would later describe it to James—in the transcript of the argument of March 14, 1882, which we will come to—as "a hunger that is never sated and a meal that is never cleared."

Her eidetic totality, as I have designated it in my formal taxonomy, was paired with the same regenerative immortality that James possessed, though in Margaret's case the discovery was less dramatic. She simply did not age. She did not fall ill. A cut sustained while coring apples in 1851 closed in seconds. By 1860, when Margaret was chronologically thirty-five and physically not a day past twenty-seven, the couple had begun to understand the scope of their situation, if not yet its implications. They understood that they would not die. They understood that Margaret would remember everything. They did not yet understand what these two facts, in combination, would do to a marriage.

The vow is the document that makes the future legible.

I reproduce it here in full, together with the marginal annotations Margaret added across subsequent decades. The annotations are datable, with some precision, by ink composition, nib width, and Margaret's own occasional habit of appending a year. I have arranged them in chronological order. The original vow text is centered; Margaret's marginalia appear to the right, with my own notes below.

---

<center>*I, Margaret, take thee, James,*</center>
<center>*to be my wedded Husband,*</center>

                                                      *So I did.* — c. 1870

<center>*to have and to hold,*</center>
<center>*from this day forward,*</center>

                                                      *And forward and forward.* — c. 1911

<center>*for better, for worse,*</center>

                                                      *Both, simultaneously, always.* — 1923

<center>*for richer, for poorer,*</center>
<center>*in sickness and in health,*</center>

                                                      *The sickness clause is void. We are obscenely well.* — c. 1939

<center>*to love and to cherish,*</center>

                                                      *I do cherish him. I also want to strangle him.* — 1964
                                                      *It wouldn't work anyway.* — 1964, same ink

<center>*till death do us part.*</center>

                                                      *Ha.* — c. 1903

---

The "Ha" is the annotation most frequently reproduced in the small body of secondary literature that has so far addressed the Greenbriar-Chen Archive.[^4] Its appeal is obvious. It is the shortest and most devastating book review ever composed: a woman's single-syllable annotation of her own marriage contract, written approximately fifty-six years into a union she has come to understand will have no exit clause. It is funny. It is also—and I find this more significant the longer I spend with the archive—not yet bitter. The bitterness comes later, and it is considerable, and it is documented with the same merciless exactitude that Margaret brought to everything. But the "Ha" of 1903 is not bitter. It is the laughter of recognition. Margaret, who by this point has watched two of her mortal siblings grow old and die while she remains physically twenty-seven, who has buried her parents and attended the funerals in heavy veils of mourning that also conveniently obscured her unlined face, who has relocated with James from Boston to Philadelphia to London to Paris, shedding identities the way other women shed winter coats—Margaret, in 1903, opens the book where she has kept her wedding vows and, upon rereading the phrase she has read a thousand times, laughs.

[^4]: See Greenbaum, "Immortality as Archive Fever" (2022); Petersen, "Involuntary Memory and the Limits of Intimate Knowledge" (2023); and one truly unfortunate article in *BuzzFeed* headlined "This 175-Year-Old Marriage Is the Most Relatable Thing You'll Read Today," which I decline to cite formally.

She sees, perhaps for the first time with full clarity, the joke that has been played on her and on James. Not by God. Not by fate. By the most ordinary sentence in the English language, which every couple repeats without hearing, because the operative word—*death*—is, for every other couple in the history of the species, a guarantee. It is the escape hatch. It is the promise that however bad it gets, the sentence is finite. Margaret, in 1903, understands that for her and James, the escape hatch has been welded shut, and the sentence is the sentence.

I note that she does not write *Ha ha*, or *How dreadful*, or append any of the elaborate commentary she affixes to other documents from this period. She writes *Ha*. A single syllable, an exhalation that is almost—but not quite—involuntary. As though the sound escaped before she could decide what she meant by it.

The later annotations are more deliberate and more layered. The 1923 note—*"Both, simultaneously, always"*—was written during the Buenos Aires period, which I will address in Section III, and which I have come to regard as the archive's most complex and most heartbreaking chapter. The 1964 notes—on cherishing and strangling—were added within minutes of each other, based on the ink's identical chemical signature, and their juxtaposition constitutes what I believe is the most honest statement on long-term marriage I have encountered in any archive, mortal or otherwise.

But it is the vow itself to which I return, and to which I will continue to return throughout this account. Margaret Greenbriar wrote it down on her wedding day because she wanted to preserve something she already knew she would remember anyway—a redundancy that tells us something essential about her character. She trusted the record more than she trusted herself. The page was meant to be a keepsake. It became a palimpsest. And the palimpsest became, across nearly two centuries of annotation, a document that is simultaneously a love letter, a bill of indictment, and the longest-running argument in the history of the Western Hemisphere.

---

## II. The Paris Apartment

In the autumn of 1872, Margaret and James Chen leased a fourth-floor apartment at 18, Rue du Cherche-Midi, in the sixth arrondissement of Paris, under the names M. et Mme. Chenier. The rental agreement, preserved in Margaret's files, specifies a term of one year with an option to renew, a monthly rent of 200 francs, a prohibition against "loud animals and professional laundering," and an expectation that tenants would maintain the window boxes.[^5] They stayed for twenty-seven years.

[^5]: Margaret's marginal note on the rental agreement: "James killed the geraniums within a month. I said nothing. I am recording this so that the record shows I said nothing."

The Paris period is, from an archival standpoint, the richest and most maddening chapter of the Greenbriar-Chen marriage, because it is the period during which both partners were producing documents at a furious rate—and producing documents that do not agree with each other about anything of significance, and agree about most trivial matters only by accident.

Margaret's record is immense. She filled eleven notebooks during the Paris years—compact, leather-bound volumes, purchased from a stationer on the Rue de Rennes—with what she called her *procès-verbaux*: transcripts of conversations, arguments, dinner parties, and daily exchanges, reproduced from memory with the fidelity of a court stenographer and the editorial instinct of a novelist. She recorded not only words but pauses, inflections, gestures, the ambient sounds of the street below, the way candlelight moved across James's face when he was trying not to say something cruel. Her transcripts have stage directions. They have footnotes. On occasion, they have what can only be described as reviews, appended after the fact in a different ink: *"I was too sharp here"* or, more frequently, *"He was insufferable and I was restrained."*

James's record, by contrast, consists of approximately forty diary entries spread across the entire twenty-seven-year period, none longer than a few sentences, most consisting of a single line, and several consisting of a single word. The entry for all of 1886 reads: *"Brussels. Rain."* They did not live in Brussels
